decks.domain: Decisions, distraction, attention and responsible driving

cards.front: How do you report road rage that is happening right now?
cards.back: Report road rage that is happening right now by calling nine one one at once.
cards.memory_hook: rage now, call nine one one

cards.front: What details should you give when reporting an aggressive driving act?
cards.back: When you call nine one one about an aggressive driving act, give where the vehicles were last seen, the plate if known, direction of travel, the road, vehicle colors, any weapons, what happened and whether you were a victim or witness.

cards.front: Why do resident reports of road rage matter?
cards.back: Cutting road rage and aggressive driving is central to the mission of the Washington State Patrol, and reports from residents help improve safety.

cards.front: Which number do you call for road rage and for witnessed aggressive driving?
cards.back: Road rage in progress goes straight to nine one one, and the same number is used to report a witnessed aggressive driving act.

decks.domain: Decisions, distraction, attention and responsible driving

cards.front: What is an informed decision, and what does it do for you?
cards.back: An informed decision weighs every factor before you act, and such decisions raise your awareness, encourage responsible driving and lower the risk of crashes.

cards.front: What three things shape your driving decisions?
cards.back: Your decisions are shaped by your knowledge of traffic laws, your experience with safe practices, and the capabilities that come with your age and brain development.

cards.front: Why must teen drivers put safety ahead of speed and peer pressure?
cards.back: In teen drivers the brain area that handles judgment and decisions is still maturing, so teens may take more risks or misjudge situations and must put safety ahead of speed and peer pressure.

cards.front: How does age affect older drivers?
cards.back: Physical and mental abilities shift with age and older drivers can be hurt more seriously in crashes, yet many stay safe and capable drivers late in life.

cards.front: Why does the guide urge extra care for teens and for older drivers?
cards.back: Teens face a still-developing judgment center in the brain, while older drivers face physical and mental changes with age, two different reasons the guide gives for extra care.

cards.front: What are the three steps of the guide's decision approach?
cards.back: The guide's decision approach has three steps: inform yourself with mirror checks and signal your plan to others, prepare the vehicle so you reach the hazard at the right position and speed, and make a final check before the maneuver.

cards.front: Where does the final check come in the decision approach?
cards.back: In the guide's decision approach the final check comes last, after informing yourself and others and after preparing your position and speed, right before the maneuver.

cards.front: What should every change you make on the road be?
cards.back: In every change you make on the road, aim to be aware, predictable and smooth.

cards.front: What are the usual ways to solve a problem on the road?
cards.back: Solving a problem on the road usually means changing your speed, shifting your lane position, or changing your path to reach a safe place to reassess, while telling others your plan so you do not surprise them.

decks.domain: Decisions, distraction, attention and responsible driving

cards.front: What does OODA stand for, and why is it a loop?
cards.back: The OODA loop is Observe, Orient, Decide, Act, and it is called a loop because each situation leads straight into the next one.

cards.front: What happens in each step of the OODA loop?
cards.back: In the OODA loop, Observe spots what changed, Orient uses your knowledge to judge what the change means for safety, Decide picks the safest action, and Act carries it out smoothly with clear signals.

cards.front: How does Observe differ from Orient?
cards.back: Observe is noticing that something changed, whereas Orient is working out what that change means for your safety and others before you Decide.

decks.domain: Decisions, distraction, attention and responsible driving

cards.front: What are the four groups of distraction?
cards.back: Distractions fall into four groups: inside the vehicle such as phones, food, the radio and passengers; outside such as billboards and crashes; physical such as fatigue or discomfort; and mental such as daydreaming, worry or strong emotion.

cards.front: Which distractions are physical, and which are mental?
cards.back: Fatigue and discomfort count as physical distractions, while daydreaming, worry and strong emotions are mental distractions, so a distraction need not involve a phone.

cards.front: What do distracted drivers tend to do?
cards.back: Distracted drivers tend to drift from their lane, drive too fast or too slow, miss signals, stop signs and vulnerable road users, and follow too closely.

cards.front: How do you avoid distraction, and what does it gain you?
cards.back: To avoid distraction, plan ahead, put the phone away and stay observant, which lets you react faster, decide better and feel less stress and fatigue.

cards.front: How does Washington define distracted driving?
cards.back: Washington defines distracted driving as any activity that pulls attention away from the main job of driving.

cards.front: May any driver hold a phone while driving, and is hands-free allowed?
cards.back: No driver of any age or experience may hold an electronic device such as a phone, tablet or gaming device while driving, though hands-free use is permitted.

cards.front: Under Washington's device law, what is the test line?
cards.back: The Washington rule bans holding any electronic device while driving for every driver, while hands-free use stays permitted, so the test line is holding, not talking.

cards.front: What can happen if you break the distracted driving law?
cards.back: An officer can ticket you for breaking the distracted driving law, the fines can be heavy, and fines for violations after your first can be doubled.

cards.front: When are distracted driving fines doubled?
cards.back: Doubling applies to distracted driving fines after your first violation, not to the first ticket itself.

decks.domain: Decisions, distraction, attention and responsible driving

cards.front: What traits do smart drivers share?
cards.back: Smart drivers are aware inside and outside the car, in control of gas, brake, steering and position, predictable through signals and smooth moves, thoughtful in decisions and intentional in learning.

cards.front: What are the four kinds of attention?
cards.back: The guide names four kinds of attention: switching from one focus to another, divided across several tasks, focused on one task, and sustained over a long time.

cards.front: How do the four kinds of attention compare?
cards.back: Switching attention jumps quickly from one thing to another, divided attention handles several things at once, focused attention puts the whole mind on one task, and sustained attention holds it over a long time.

cards.front: How can you help your attention while driving?
cards.back: Help your attention by removing in-car distractions, being well rested, silencing and stowing electronics, limiting passengers and pets, and refusing to multitask.

decks.domain: Decisions, distraction, attention and responsible driving

cards.front: What is the difference between searching and scanning?
cards.back: Searching means actively checking around you with your eyes, while scanning adds turning your head, neck and body to see as much as possible.

cards.front: How does searching differ from scanning?
cards.back: Searching uses your eyes alone to check around you, while scanning also moves your head, neck and body to widen what you can see.

cards.front: How fast should you drive in relation to searching and scanning?
cards.back: Drive at a speed that still lets you search and scan well, because constant searching underpins safe driving.

cards.front: What should you watch for when scanning ahead?
cards.back: Scanning ahead means watching for things to steer around, blockages that could hide people, feet, wheels or shadows near parked cars, and what is happening beyond the car in front, so you avoid sudden braking or swerving.

cards.front: What should you watch for when scanning to the side?
cards.back: Scanning to the side means watching left and right at intersections, watching for crossing walkers and cyclists, watching for movement behind foliage, and doing a mirror and over-shoulder check before turning.

cards.front: When should you look for vehicles and cyclists behind you?
cards.back: Look for vehicles and cyclists behind you before a lane change, before turning across a bike lane, and when slowing, backing, or heading down a long or steep hill.

cards.front: Why look behind more often in heavy traffic?
cards.back: Look behind more often in heavy traffic so that a tailgater or fast-approaching vehicle gives you time to react by changing lanes, tapping the brakes, or adjusting speed.

decks.domain: Decisions, distraction, attention and responsible driving

cards.front: What does respectful driving include?
cards.back: Respectful driving means everyone buckled up, being fit to drive, showing empathy, respecting others' space, avoiding conflict no matter who is at fault, and caring for the road environment.

cards.front: What are traffic advisories, and how are they delivered?
cards.back: Traffic advisories are alerts about current or coming conditions, incidents or closures from transportation officials, traffic centers or navigation apps, delivered by electronic road signs, radio, websites, social media and apps.

cards.front: Why are littering fines severe, and what must you and passengers do?
cards.back: Road litter can cause crashes and burning litter can start wildfires, so Washington's littering fines are severe and you and your passengers must secure loads and dispose of trash properly.

cards.front: How do state and local littering rules relate?
cards.back: State law sets minimum fines for littering and illegal dumping, and local ordinances may differ, so ask local police, the sheriff or a city or county clerk which rules apply.

cards.front: What does state law fix about littering fines?
cards.back: State law fixes only the minimum littering fines, and cities and counties may set their own different rules on top of it.

cards.front: Why should you not leave a parked car running?
cards.back: Leaving a parked car running, especially inside a garage, can release deadly carbon monoxide, so shut the engine off when parked a while, drive smoothly, keep tires inflated and carpool when you can.

cards.front: What does Washington's Clean Car Law require?
cards.back: Washington's Clean Car Law says a vehicle built in two thousand nine or later must pass strict clean air standards before anyone can register, license or sell it.

cards.front: Which vehicles does the Clean Car Law cover, and what does it block?
cards.back: The Clean Car Law covers vehicles built in two thousand nine and later and blocks registering, licensing or selling one that fails the clean air standards.

cards.front: What questions help you evaluate your own driving?
cards.back: After or during a drive, evaluate yourself by asking whether anything surprised you, whether you surprised anyone, whether your driving was legal, proficient and smooth, and what to change next time, because skills fade without review.

recap_hooks.text: Call nine one one for road rage in progress or a witnessed aggressive act, and give location, plate, direction and what happened.
Resident reports help the State Patrol improve safety.
Informed decisions weigh every factor and draw on knowledge, experience and development.
Teens put safety ahead of speed and peer pressure, and many older drivers stay capable.
Inform, prepare, then make a final check, staying aware, predictable and smooth.
Observe, Orient, Decide, Act, and the loop starts again.
Distractions can be inside, outside, physical or mental, and they make you drift and miss things.
Never hold a device while driving; hands-free is allowed, and repeat fines can double.
Smart drivers are aware, in control and predictable, and use four kinds of attention.
Searching uses your eyes; scanning adds your head and body, at a speed that allows it.
Scan ahead, to the sides and behind, more often in heavy traffic.
Drive with respect, use traffic advisories, and secure loads and trash.
Avoid idling, follow the Clean Car Law and review your own driving.
